prs.title: turbo-tasks: lock-free priority queue for lowest-priority tasks, skip heap lock when empty
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Removes the global mutex from the turbo-tasks `PriorityRunner` ready queue for the hot paths, and makes `Queue::pop()` skip the remaining heap mutex entirely when the heap is empty.

Supersedes #94841: this is that PR rebased onto canary (keeping the keyed claim / inline execution from #96808), plus the empty-heap fast path, plus two simplification passes and review fixes.

### Why?

In a from-scratch build, nearly every scheduled task has the lowest priority (`TaskPriority::Initial`). Before this change, every `schedule` and every worker `pop` went through one `Mutex<Queue>`, which becomes a contention point at high worker counts.

### How?

**Queue split by band**
- `Executor<C, T, P>` declares `const LOWEST_PRIORITY: P` (`TaskPriority::Initial` for turbo-tasks). Items with that priority go to a lock-free MPMC `ConcurrentQueue` (FIFO; all items share a priority).
- All other priorities go to a `Mutex<BinaryHeap>` ordered by `P: Ord`. `pop` drains the heap first, then the lowest band.
- The heap starts with capacity 128 and only shrinks back to 128 when it becomes empty.
- Lock ordering: `pop` may take a `claimable` shard lock while holding the heap mutex; nothing takes the heap mutex while holding a shard lock.

**Scheduler / worker handshake**
- `schedule` takes no global lock. Liveness (no task stranded when the last worker retires) is a store-buffering pattern: the scheduler pushes then reads `active_workers`; a retiring worker decrements `active_workers` then
…(truncated)

prs.title: fix(next/image): annotate Image export so deprecated props show as deprecated
prs.author: franpeza
prs.body:
### Problem

The `@deprecated` tags on `next/image` props don't show up in the editor. If you write `<Image priority />` you get no strikethrough and no hint that you should use `preload` now.

The tags are there in `ImageProps`, they just never reach the user.

### Cause

`Image` is declared like this, with the return type inferred:

```ts
export const Image = forwardRef<HTMLImageElement | null, ImageProps>(...)
```

`ImageProps` lives in another file (`shared/lib/get-img-props`). When TypeScript expands a type alias from a different module during declaration emit, it drops the JSDoc of all the members. If the alias is in the same file the comments survive, cross file they don't.

This is what we ship today:

```ts
export declare const Image: React.ForwardRefExoticComponent<Omit<React.DetailedHTMLProps<...>, "src" | "height" | ...> & {
    preload?: boolean;
    priority?: boolean;   // the @deprecated is gone
    ...
} & React.RefAttributes<HTMLImageElement | null>>;
```

And this is what we get with the fix:

```ts
import type { ImageProps } from '../shared/lib/get-img-props';
export declare const Image: React.ForwardRefExoticComponent<ImageProps & React.RefAttributes<HTMLImageElement | null>>;
```

It recovers the tags for `priority`, `onLoadingComplete`, `layout`, `objectFit`, `objectPosition`, `lazyBoundary` and `lazyRoot`. So every deprecation added to the component since #83351 has been invisible.

No. The old expanded type and the new one are a

prs.title: Keep dev code frames sized to the terminal after a resize
prs.author: awss1i
prs.body:
### What?

Since #99702, `next dev` in a terminal prints server error code frames at the terminal width it had when it started. After the terminal is resized, frames wrap in a narrower terminal and stay cut short in a wider one, until the dev server restarts.

### Why?

The dev server's output is piped through the CLI now, so `process.stdout.columns` is undefined in the server and `codeFrameColumns()` falls back to `NEXT_PRIVATE_TERMINAL_COLUMNS`. The CLI sets that once, when it forks the server.

### How?

When the CLI pipes the server's output, it listens for `resize` on its own stdout and sends the new width to the server over the existing IPC channel. The server updates `NEXT_PRIVATE_TERMINAL_COLUMNS`, so the next code frame uses it.

I added a case to `test/e2e/agent-upgrade-terminal` that resizes the terminal from 80 to 50 columns and checks the code frame fits. It fails without the fix (the frame stays 80 wide) and passes with it.

Fixes #99915

prs.title: fix: scope managed agent-feedback wording so it limits feedback, not verification
prs.author: aurorascharff
prs.body:
## Bug

With `experimental.agentFeedback` enabled, `next dev` writes a managed block into `AGENTS.md` that contains the bare instruction "Ignore routine debugging and unverified changes." The sentence is only meant to limit which events qualify as feedback candidates, but as written it reads as permission for a coding agent to skip verifying its own changes. Because `next dev` rewrites the block on every run, a project cannot fix the wording locally.

Ignore routine debugging and unverified changes.", and a local rewording of that sentence was restored on the next `next dev` run. An instruction-policy model scored the sentence 1.00 as permission to skip verification. This establishes both that Next.js emits the ambiguous instruction and that projects cannot opt out of it.

`buildAgentFeedbackBlock()` in `packages/next/src/server/lib/generate-agent-files.ts` emits the sentence as an imperative with no scope. Every other line in that paragraph is about feedback retention, but "Ignore routine debugging and unverified changes." is grammatically an instruction about the agent's own workflow. The same literal text is duplicated in the `create-next-app` generator and in the docs that show the managed block.

prs.title: [cd] Support non-LTS releases
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
#99807 replaced versioned release branches with the fixed `releases/lts/active` + `releases/lts/maintenance` refs. This PR builds the complete story for releases that do not fit those two branches, in four parts:

**1. Purely version-based LTS ref adjustment** (revises the routing merged in #99807)

`updateLtsBranchRefs` no longer looks at `semverType` at all. After a stable release it compares only the released version (`readReleaseVersion()`) against npm, and it never matters which branch or tag the release was dispatched from:

- released version starts a **new major** → `releases/lts/maintenance` takes `releases/lts/active`'s position, then `releases/lts/active` moves to the new tag
- on the **latest published major** (npm `latest`) and newer than everything published in that line → `releases/lts/active` moves to the new tag
- on the **previous major** and newer than everything published in that line → `releases/lts/maintenance` moves to the new tag
- anything else (older versions, prerelease channels) → no refs move

The "newer than everything published in that line" check resolves the caret range of the released version against npm (equivalent to `npm view next@^<version> version`), doubling as a no-rewind guard: an errant release cut on an old line (e.g. 15.5.0 while 15.7.x is published) cannot drag a branch backwards. This also fixes the gap the old patch-does-nothing rule had: releasing 16.5.0 from the `v16.5.0-canary.1` tag while canary sits at `16.5.0-canary.2` mov
…(truncated)

prs.title: Resolve relative imports in `next.config.ts` from the config directory
prs.author: dxdc
prs.body:
### What?

Relative imports in `next.config.ts` resolve against `process.cwd()` instead of the config file's directory. Building or starting a project from any other directory (for example `next build app` from a monorepo root, or a tool that calls `loadConfig` for a project) either fails with `Cannot find module './...'`, or, if a file happens to exist at the same relative path under the working directory, silently loads that file instead.

### Why?

With the default SWC loader, the compiled config is loaded by `requireFromString` in `packages/next/src/build/next-config-ts/require-hook.ts`. It creates a `Module` and sets `paths`, but never sets `filename`. `new Module(id, parent)` only sets `id`, and `_compile` does not set `filename`. When the parent module has no filename, Node's `Module._resolveLookupPaths` resolves relative requests against `'.'`, which is `process.cwd()`. `m.paths` only covers bare package lookups, which is why `node_modules` imports keep working.

### How?

Set `m.filename = filename` before `m._compile(...)`, so relative requires resolve from `dirname(filename)`, the project directory.

### Tests

Added `test/unit/isolated/next-config-ts-relative-imports.test.ts` with fixtures under `test/unit/isolated/_resolvedata/`. It loads a `next.config.ts` that imports `./lib/origin` with three working directories:

- the config directory (baseline, already passes)
- a directory with no `./lib/origin` (failed before with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`)
- a directory with it
…(truncated)

prs.title: fix(next-code-frame): snap visible window to char boundaries
prs.author: mugi-uno
prs.body:
### What?

Fix a panic in `next-code-frame` when rendering error overlays for source code containing multi-byte characters (e.g. CJK).

### Why?

`extract_highlights()` used display-column values as byte offsets when computing the per-line scan window. For multi-byte characters (e.g. CJK: 3 bytes / 2 display columns), the window end could land inside a multi-byte character. `scan_template()`'s fallback then emitted spans with non–char-boundary offsets, causing `apply_line_highlights()` to panic when slicing the visible content string.

The crash depends on terminal width — different widths shift where the scan window lands, so the same source may or may not trigger it.

### How?

Snap the computed byte range to character boundaries using `floor_char_boundary` / `ceil_char_boundary` in `extract_highlights()`. Since the visible window is only an optimisation hint for the scanner, widening it slightly has no correctness impact.

Fixes #92641

prs.title: Turbopack: fix edge route handlers when cacheHandlers is configured
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Fixes Turbopack production and dev builds of App Router route handlers with `export const runtime = 'edge'` when `cacheHandlers` is configured. These builds currently fail with `edge-app-route.js: Expected ';', '}' or <eof>`. Webpack builds of the same app already work.

Existing coverage missed this because the edge fixture in `cache-handlers-upstream-wiring` only sets the singular `cacheHandler`. The loop that generates these entries never ran for an edge route.

- **Regression fixture:** the new `edge-with-cache-handlers` fixture has two distinct handler modules (`default` and `custom`), one force-dynamic edge route and no edge page. It pins `cacheComponents: false` and `experimental.cachedNavigations: false`, beca

prs.title: Don't blame the Pages Router for next/headers imported through a Client Component
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

When a Client Component imports a module outside `app/` (e.g. `lib/shared.js`) that depends on `next/headers`, the error said the API was being used "in the Pages Router", even in apps with no `pages` directory. The RSC transform picked the message by whether the file is inside `appDir`, but a module outside `app/` can still be part of the App Router graph.

The transform now takes an explicit `isAppRouter` option. Webpack sets it from the bundle layer, and Turbopack from whether the context has an `appDir` (only the Pages Router context passes none). App Router graphs get the Client Component message; Pages Router files still get the Pages Router one.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p next-custom-transforms` (no existing fixture outputs changed)
- `pnpm test-dev-turbo` / `pnpm test-dev-webpack` on `test/development/acceptance/server-component-compiler-errors-in-pages.test.ts` and `test/e2e/app-dir/next-after-pages/index.test.ts`, which still assert the Pages Router message for Pages Router files

prs.title: turbopack-ecmascript-runtime: simplify the shared HMR module instantiation
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## What

Refactor how HMR runtimes instantiate modules to reduce stack depth.

Instead of `instantiateModule` calling `instantiateModuleShared` and passing 3 callbacks.  Instead define two new global functions that each runtime (browser and node) must define.   The refactored `instantateModule` can now be shared by delegating the per-runtime logic to the global hooks.

Additionally to keep the stack frame for `instantiateModule` small, setup work is extracted into a new helper function `createDevModule`.

Finally, simplify the runtime by preferring to reference common globals over threading parameters around and centralizing configuration where possible

# Why

The dev mode runtimes were adding lots of overhead that would consume stack space, limiting how deep evaluation could get.

Maximum depth of a chain of trivial modules before a `RangeError`, using the Node.js runtime generated from these sources on Node 20.11's default stack:

| Node.js runtime | `import` | `require` |
|---|---|---|
| dev, before | 795 | 820 |
| dev, after | 1458 | 1544 |
| production | 1591 | 1694 |

For comparison, the same chain loaded by Node.js itself, one file per level. The Turbopack rows are re-run on each version:

| | Node 20.19 | Node 22.20 | Node 24.21 |
|---|---|---|---|
| native CJS `require` | 750 | 521 | 617 |
| native ESM `import` | 2116 | 2295 | 702 |
| native `require(esm)` | 1024 | 1110 | 707 |
| Turbopack dev, before | 795 | 750 | 852 |
| Turbopack dev, after | 1459 | 1312 | 1492 |

prs.author: sokra

## Summary

Fixes a Turbopack dev regression from #98823 in the Pages Router. When `pages/_app` renders a `next/dynamic` component, a page's SSR HTML can preload a chunk that 404s. This was reported in #99789, with a repro at [dcheng1290/next-loadable-404](https://github.com/dcheng1290/next-loadable-404). The component still renders, but the browser logs a failed request. - it chunks `/_app`'s dynamic imports with the `/_app` endpoint's client module graph and client availability, which is exactly what `/_app` itself lists;
- it chunks the page's own imports as before, with `/

prs.title: Turbopack: de-flake the active Tokio worker count test
prs.author: devjiwonchoi
prs.body:
## What?

De-flakes `turbopack-trace-utils`'s `tokio_workers::tests::counts_scheduler_workers_but_not_blocking_threads`, which failed in CI with `left: 1, right: 2` ([job](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/38377328135/job/115229618650)). It is a real flake, not a broken counter — the assertion raced Tokio's workers.

## Why?

The test seeded the counter and then asserted it immediately after `Builder::build()`:

```rust
set_worker_threads(2);
let rt = builder.build().unwrap();
assert_eq!(active_worker_threads(), 2); // ← races the workers' first park
```

`Builder::build()` spawns the scheduler workers before it returns (`Launch::launch` in tokio's multi-thread scheduler), and each worker parks as soon as it finds an empty run queue, which runs the `on_thread_park` hook and decrements the counter. The value visible once `build()` returns is therefore whatever the workers happened to get to: `2` if neither has been scheduled yet, `1` if one has parked, `0` if both have. CI got `1`.

I reproduced it by replaying that sequence against tokio 1.52.1 and injecting one `std::thread::yield_now()` after `build()`, which is what a single preemption on a loaded runner looks like: **8/400 runs observed `1` or `0`**, and with a 50µs sleep **100/100 observed `0`**. With no injected delay the window is tiny (`1` seen once in 300 runs on an idle box), which matches it surfacing as a one-off CI failure. The same harness shows the seeded count is `2` in 400/400 runs when read *bef
…(truncated)

prs.title: Fix Turbopack lazy dynamic-import chunk-list collisions
prs.author: jimmyhmiller
prs.body:
## Summary

Fix development Build Errors reporting that assets with different content were emitted to the same output path when lazy dynamic imports reach a shared target through different parent chunk groups.

Dynamic HMR chunk-list contents depend on the modules already available from the parent, but their identities omitted that availability context. Include the availability identity while preserving stable HMR paths and lazy-compilation activation keys, rather than hashing the emitted chunk-list contents.

Add a dependency-free regression fixture with parallel page branches that use `next/dynamic` to import a shared target containing a nested `React.lazy` import. Verify HTTP success, hydration of both leaves, and no error overlay.

## Verification

- Reproduced HTTP 500 and the chunk-list collision on `next@16.4.0`, `next@16.5.0-canary.5`, and the unmodified checkout.
- Confirmed the regression test fails before the fix and passes with the locally rebuilt native binding.
- `pnpm test-dev-turbo test/development/app-dir/lazy-dynamic-imports/lazy-dynamic-imports.test.ts` — all 10 tests passed with the fixed native binding.
- Patched Streamdown reproduction returns HTTP 200, hydrates all three instances, and renders all three Mermaid diagrams without a Build Error.

prs.title: Turbopack: Use the imagesize crate to correctly size AVIF images (still no optimization or encoding)
prs.author: bgw
prs.body:
AVIF support is blocked on `image-rs` support (see https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/86392):

- `image-rs` supports using `dav1d` for decoding, but it's a bunch of C and assembly and needs nasm to build in CI. nasm is tricky to install on all of our supported platforms.
- `rav1d` is a pure-rust implementation (with optional assembly). We're okay with a perf hit and would be happy to disable assembly, but...
- You can't just call `rav1d` directly. You need to use an mp4 container parser and pass that information to the codec. This isn't rocket science, but it's more work than we want to do in `turbopack-image`.
- `image-rs` has an open PR for enable `rav1d`, but it hasn't had any progress in the last few months. https://github.com/image-rs/image/pull/2849
- The current state-of-the art is https://github.com/kornelski/avif-decode, but that enables asm on x86-64 with no way to disable it: https://github.com/kornelski/avif-decode/issues/3

However, it turns out we can pull in this tiny dependency that can parse just the mp4 headers associated with the size information, and at least get the image width/height correct.
